properties.name: Rome
properties.one_line: Trajan's moneyers struck the gold aurei, silver denarii, and bronze sestertii that funded the Dacian and Parthian wars from the mint near the Capitoline. Every provincial city that struck its own coin copied the portrait these dies set. In 117 CE it was the single busiest mint in the Mediterranean world.
sources: RIC II (Roman Imperial Coinage, Trajan)
NGC Ancients: Mints of the Roman Empire, ngccoin.com/news/article/8151
Ostia-Antica.org, 'The Maxentian Mint at Ostia' (Rome mint topography note)

properties.name: Lyon
properties.one_line: Augustus opened Lugdunum as the empire's second mint in 15 BCE, and for nearly a century it struck gold and silver alongside Rome. Its last major precious-metal issue ran under Vespasian in the 70s CE, and by Trajan's reign the workshop sat dormant, its output folded entirely into Rome. It stayed idle for another 180 years, until Diocletian revived it in 297 CE.
sources: NGC Ancients: Mints of the Roman Empire, ngccoin.com/news/article/8151
Aeternitas Numismatics, 'Knowing the Roman imperial mints: VIII - Lugdunum', aeternitas-numismatics.com
Cambridge, Journal of Roman Studies, 'The Mints of the Empire: Vespasian to Diocletian'

properties.name: Antioch
properties.one_line: Antioch struck silver tetradrachms bearing Trajan's portrait to pay the legions massing for his Parthian invasion, each coin stamped with an eagle gripping a club on the reverse. With Hadrian stationed here as governor of Syria, the city functioned as the empire's forward capital in 117 CE.
sources: RPC III (Nerva-Hadrian), Antioch, Syria
McAlee, R., The Coinage of Antioch
Ancient Coin Traders, Trajan AR Tetradrachm, Antioch 98-99 CE, RPC/Prieur plate coin

properties.name: Alexandria
properties.one_line: Alexandria ran Egypt's closed currency system, striking billon tetradrachms that were illegal to carry across the province's border. Anyone arriving had to trade denarii for local coin at the frontier. Trajan's tetradrachm issue turned out to be the only major Egyptian silver coinage of the entire second century.
sources: Howgego, C., 'Coinage and the Roman Economy in the Antonine Period: the view from Egypt', Oxford Roman Economy Project, oxrep.classics.ox.ac.uk
Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2005.07.64, 'Coinage in Roman Egypt: The Hoard Evidence'

properties.name: Caesarea
properties.one_line: Caesarea, seat of Judaea's Roman governor, struck its own bronze coinage showing Tyche crowned with a city wall and altars to the emperor. A dated issue from around 115 CE proves the mint was still running just before the Kitos War tore through the province.
sources: RPC III 3954, Trajan, Caesarea Maritima AE
Wikipedia, 'Procuratorial coinage of Roman Judaea'

properties.name: Kayseri
properties.one_line: Caesarea in Cappadocia ran the largest provincial mint outside Alexandria, striking silver drachms and didrachms to pay the legions guarding the Armenian frontier. Its heaviest Trajanic issue, three light tetradrachm types struck in 112-114 CE during his sixth consulship, pictured Mount Argaeus and a kneeling camel of Arabia.
sources: Butcher, K. & Ponting, M., Numismatic Chronicle 175 (2015), silver coinage of Cappadocia, warwick.ac.uk offprint
Vcoins, Trajan AR Drachm, Caesarea Cappadocia, Arabia standing type

properties.name: Izmit
properties.one_line: Nicomedia, metropolis of Bithynia, was one of about fourteen city mints striking bronze coin across the province under Trajan. Each coin carried the emperor's portrait on one face and a local civic type on the other, part of a regional currency system that ran parallel to Rome's.
sources: Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2024.07.03, 'Between Roman culture and local tradition: Roman provincial coinage of Bithynia and Pontus during the reign of Trajan (98-117 AD)'
Academia.edu, 'The Roman Imperial Coinage Model for Some Provincial Coins of Bithynia and Pontus Struck During the Reign of Trajan (98-117)'

properties.name: Pergamon
properties.one_line: Pergamon's mint had struck the broad silver cistophorus since the 2nd century BCE, and Rome kept the coin alive as Asia's standard high-value currency, worth three denarii. Trajan's moneyers continued the type through his reign, carrying forward a design older than the province itself.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Cistophorus'
American Numismatic Society, 'Attalid Cistophori and Roman Foreign Affairs in Asia Minor', numismatics.org/pocketchange/attalids
Academia.edu, 'The Introduction of Roman Coinages in Asia (133 BC-1st Century AD)'

properties.name: Ephesus
properties.one_line: Ephesus shared cistophorus production with Pergamon as one of only two workshops supplying Asia's silver currency, its busy harbor making it the easiest point to ship new coin around the province. Its own civic bronze ran alongside, stamped with the names of local magistrates each year.
sources: Forum Ancient Coins discussion board, 'The Coinage of Ephesus'
Coin World, 'Cistophori of Roman emperor Hadrian began with overstriking of older coins'
Wikipedia, 'Cistophorus'

properties.name: Smyrna
properties.one_line: Smyrna ran a civic bronze mint under local magistrates and sophists, its dies carrying Zeus Akraios from his temple on Mount Pagus and the city's twin patron goddesses, the Nemeses. The mint's output continued without interruption through Trajan's nineteen-year reign.
sources: RPC III (Smyrna civic issues, Nerva-Hadrian)
Art Institute of Chicago, 'Coin Depicting the God Zeus Akraios'
Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 'Coin of Smyrna with bust of Zeus Akraios'

properties.name: Sardis
properties.one_line: Sardis, where Lydian kings first struck coinage some seven centuries earlier, kept its own civic bronze mint running through the Roman principate. Its Roman-era coins paired the emperor's portrait with local Lydian imagery, a small echo of the city's ancient monetary fame.
sources: Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2019.06.19, 'Coins from the Excavations at Sardis'
RPC Online I 2997a
Numista, 'The Bronze Coinage of Lydia, Sardes (Sardis), Tripolis'

properties.name: Tarsus
properties.one_line: Tarsus struck silver tetradrachms under Trajan pairing the emperor's bust with Tyche and the river-god Cydnus, the waterway running through the city's center. Cilicia's leading city was one of the few provincial mints trusted with silver rather than bronze alone.
sources: RPC II 754, Trajan, Tarsus AR Tetradrachm
Ancient Numismatic Mythology, 'Coinage of Cilicia', ancientcoinage.org

properties.name: Iznik
properties.one_line: Nicaea struck bronze coins under Trajan showing an altar on the reverse, one of roughly a dozen Bithynian cities licensed to mint their own small change. The city's rivalry with neighboring Nicomedia for the title of Bithynia's leading city played out partly through competing coin types.
sources: RPC III 1154 and 1059, Trajan, Nicaea
Academia.edu, 'Coins of the Bithynian Mint of Nicaea from the Viminacium Necropolis of Pecine'

properties.name: Apamea Cibotus
properties.one_line: Apamea, founded around 270 BCE by the Seleucid king Antiochus I and known to Romans as Cibotus, kept a civic bronze mint running into Trajan's reign under local high priests named on the coin legends. The city sat at a major road junction in Phrygia, feeding the wider trade that filled its treasury.
sources: Numista, 'Items from Apamea (Phrygia)'
Forum Ancient Coins, 'Ancient Greek Coins of Phrygia'

properties.name: Laodicea on the Lycus
properties.one_line: Laodicea, a wool and banking city so wealthy it rebuilt itself after a major earthquake without imperial aid, struck civic bronze honoring Trajan's wife Plotina as Augusta, a title she held from 105 CE. That dated issue fixes the mint's activity squarely within Trajan's reign.
sources: RPC III 2320, Plotina, Laodicea ad Lycum
Numista, 'Items from Laodicea ad Lycum'

properties.name: Tripoli
properties.one_line: Tripolis took its name from the three Phoenician cities, Tyre, Sidon, and Arados, that jointly founded it, and it kept a semi-autonomous civic mint striking small bronze coin for local trade. Its types carried Tyche and the twin caps of the Dioskuri, symbols the city had used since the Hellenistic era.
sources: WildWinds.com, 'Phoenicia, Tripolis'
Forum Ancient Coins, 'Tripolis'

properties.name: Tyre
properties.one_line: Tyre's mint had gone silent for silver since Nero ended its famous shekel series in 65 CE, but Trajan revived it, striking tetradrachms again through his reign and into Hadrian's first year. The renewed coins carried an eagle gripping a club, no longer branded as an independent city issue but struck explicitly for the emperor.
sources: Coin World, 'The Shekels of Tyre: Ancients Today'
WildWinds.com, 'Phoenicia, Tyre'
Grokipedia, 'Tyrian shekel'

properties.name: Sidon
properties.one_line: Sidon struck civic bronze without a break for close to a century and a half, from Augustus through Hadrian, naming itself sacred and inviolate in its coin legends. Its types ranged from Tyche and Zeus to war galleys and Astarte riding in her sacred cart.
sources: Forum Ancient Coins NumisWiki, 'phoenicia'
WildWinds.com, 'Sidon, Phoenicia'

properties.name: Beirut
properties.one_line: Berytus, a Roman colony settled by veterans of two legions under Augustus and grown to roughly 50,000 people by Trajan's reign, struck its own bronze coinage showing a priest yoking oxen, the standard emblem of a newly founded colony. A dated issue survives from within Trajan's 98-117 reign.
sources: WildWinds.com, 'Berytos, Phoenicia'
Forum Ancient Coins NumisWiki, 'berytus'

properties.name: Ashkelon
properties.one_line: Ascalon opened Trajan's reign with a fresh bronze issue in its own civic year 129, equal to 98 CE, showing Nike striding with a palm branch and wreath. The free city counted its years from its own charter of freedom rather than Rome's calendar, advertising the autonomy its coinage represented.
sources: Forum Ancient Coins, 'Pseudo-Autonomous Roman Provincial Coins'

properties.name: Cyzicus
properties.one_line: Cyzicus struck its own bronze coinage under Trajan from a mint beside the isthmus linking the Kapidag peninsula to the Mysian mainland. Its dies paired the emperor's portrait with local gods like Kore Soteira across dozens of distinct Trajanic types. The city's harbor made it one of the busiest ports on the Sea of Marmara, feeding trade for the whole province of Asia.
sources: RPC III 1485-1496, Trajan, Cyzicus AE
Aeternitas Numismatics, 'Knowing the Roman imperial mints: VII - Cyzicus'
properties.image_credit: Ruins of Cyzicus, Erdek, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Bursa
properties.one_line: Prusa ad Olympum, set on the northern slopes of Mount Olympus of Mysia, struck civic bronze coin under Trajan as one of fourteen minting cities across Bithynia and Pontus. Its coins carried the emperor's portrait on one face and local river gods on the other, following the same regional currency system as neighboring Nicaea and Nicomedia. The mint sat idle for long stretches before and after his reign, so its Trajanic issues survive as some of the rarest coins the city ever struck.
sources: RPC III 1035-1049, Trajan, Prusa ad Olympum
Harvard Art Museums, 'Coin of Prusa ad Olympum under Trajan'
properties.image_credit: Roman sculpture, Bursa Archaeological Museum · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Bosra
properties.one_line: Trajan's general Cornelius Palma folded the Nabataean kingdom into Rome in 106 CE, and the new provincial capital took the name Nova Trajana Bostra in his honor. Its mint struck silver tridrachms and drachms stamped with a camel, the animal that had carried the region's incense trade for centuries. Legio III Cyrenaica garrisoned the city, guarding the new Via Traiana Nova running south all the way to the Red Sea.
sources: RPC III 4060, 4075, 4076, Trajan, Bostra
Wikipedia, 'Via Traiana Nova'
properties.image_credit: Roman theatre, Bosra, Syria · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Sepphoris
properties.one_line: Sepphoris, the largest city in Galilee, struck its first city-coinage under Trajan, stamping a palm tree flanked by two bunches of dates on the reverse of its bronze. The Greek legend on the obverse recorded that the emperor himself had granted the city this right. That grant did not last long: minting stopped before his reign ended, likely a penalty for the city's role in the 115-117 revolt, and coin did not flow from Sepphoris again until Antoninus Pius.
sources: RPC III 3936, Trajan, Sepphoris (Diocaesarea)
Judaism and Rome, 'City-Coin of Sepphoris depicting the head of Trajan and a palm tree'
CoinWeek, David Hendin, 'Coins Tell the Story of Ancient Sepphoris'
properties.image_credit: Dionysus mosaic floor, Sepphoris, Israel · Wikimedia Commons (photo Carole Raddato, CC BY-SA)

properties.name: Hierapolis
properties.one_line: Hierapolis, famous even in antiquity for its blinding white travertine terraces, struck civic bronze under Trajan showing Athena standing beside Hermes with his money-bag and caduceus. The mint had been running since the 2nd century BCE, long before Rome arrived in Asia. A sacred hot spring fed the city's baths and gave the site its reputation as a place where gods and healing waters met.
sources: RPC I 2982 and RPC III (Trajan-period issues), Hierapolis, Phrygia
WildWinds.com, 'Phrygia, Hierapolis'
properties.image_credit: Ruins of Hierapolis, Pamukkale, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Perge
properties.one_line: Perge struck bronze under Trajan showing a temple front holding the cult statue of Artemis Pergaia with an eagle in the pediment, plus a smaller issue pairing his portrait with a harbor prow and lighthouse. The river Cestrus carried ships two miles inland to reach the city's gates. Perge's games and processions honoring Artemis drew visitors from across Pamphylia every year.
sources: RPC III 2689, Trajan, Perge
SNG Copenhagen 315, Trajan, Perge
properties.image_credit: Overview of the ruins of Perge, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Ankara
properties.one_line: Ancyra struck semi-autonomous bronze coin under Trajan, whose armies marched through the city in 113 CE on their way to the Parthian front, the first emperor known to have passed through it in person. The walls of its Temple of Augustus and Rome, built decades earlier, still carried the full engraved text of the Res Gestae, Augustus's own account of his reign, letting any literate visitor read the deified founder's memoir in stone. Galatia's capital sat at the crossroads where roads from the Bosphorus, the Black Sea, and Cappadocia all met.
sources: RPC III 3115, Ankyra, Galatia, semi-autonomous AE
Livius.org, 'Ancyra (Ankara)'
Wikipedia, 'Temple of Augustus and Rome'
properties.image_credit: Temple of Augustus and Rome, Ankara, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons (photo Carole Raddato, CC BY-SA)

properties.name: Samsun
properties.one_line: Amisus struck bronze under Trajan showing Nike striding with a palm branch and wreath, coinage issued long after the mint's earlier heyday under the Kings of Pontus. The free city had kept the right to strike its own coin as a reward for backing Rome during the Mithridatic Wars two centuries before. Its harbor made it the commercial capital of the entire province of Pontus.
sources: RPC I 2145, 2154; RPC II 729, Trajan, Amisus
Wikipedia, 'Coinage of Amisos' (historical context)
properties.image_credit: Display case, Samsun Archaeology Museum, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Sinop
properties.one_line: Sinope, a Roman colony since Julius Caesar planted veterans there, struck bronze under Trajan alongside the dozen other city mints of Bithynia and Pontus. Its Roman-era bathhouse, later converted into the Balatlar church, still stands with walls thick enough to have survived two thousand years of Black Sea storms. Diogenes the Cynic, the philosopher who supposedly lived in a barrel, was born in this same harbor town almost five centuries earlier.
sources: RPC III 1217-1219, Trajan, Sinope
Wikipedia, 'Balatlar Church'
properties.image_credit: Balatlar Church, a Roman-era bath building, Sinop, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Cyrene
properties.one_line: Cyrene struck silver hemidrachms and bronze coin under Trajan pairing his portrait with the horned head of Zeus Ammon, the oracle god whose desert shrine had drawn pilgrims for seven centuries. An earthquake struck the region hard in 115 CE, badly damaging the city's Temple of Zeus even as its mint kept striking coin through the rest of the reign. Jewish rebels devastated much of Cyrenaica the following year in the Kitos War.
sources: RPC III 3, Trajan, Cyrene AR Hemidrachm
Wikipedia, 'Temple of Zeus, Cyrene'
properties.image_credit: Temple of Zeus, Cyrene, Libya · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Paphos
properties.one_line: The Koinon of Cyprus, the island's confederation of cities, struck bronze coin under Trajan stamped with the conical black stone of the Temple of Aphrodite at Paphos, the goddess's most sacred shrine anywhere in the ancient world. Metal analysis shows these Trajanic issues were struck from dies cut in Rome and shipped out for use on the island. Paphos itself served as the political capital of Roman Cyprus, and its Houses of Dionysos and Theseus already carried some of the mosaic floors still visible today.
sources: Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 'Coin of Koinon of Cyprus with bust of Trajan'
Kyprios Character, 'Cypriote coinage under Roman rule (30 BC - 3rd century AD)'
properties.image_credit: Roman mosaics, Paphos Archaeological Park, Cyprus · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Amasra
properties.one_line: Amastris took shape when four smaller Paphlagonian towns merged under a Persian-descended queen who gave the new city her name, and it was still striking its own bronze four centuries later under Trajan. Its Trajanic issues carried the war god Ares on one type and the personification Hope on another, part of a set of motifs it shared with neighboring Nicaea and Nicomedia. Twin harbors on a narrow peninsula made the town one of the safest anchorages on the whole Black Sea coast.
sources: RPC III 1198-1208, Trajan, Amastris
properties.image_credit: Amasra (ancient Amastris), Turkey · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Prusias ad Hypium
properties.one_line: Prusias ad Hypium, renamed from Cierus for the Bithynian king who once ruled it, struck civic bronze under Trajan showing the goddess Pax on its reverse. Its Roman theater, carved into the hillside above the Hypius river valley, is still largely intact and open to visitors today. The city stood along the inland road linking the Bithynian coast to the interior of Asia Minor.
sources: RPC III 1101-1103, Trajan, Prusias ad Hypium
Wikipedia, 'Prusias ad Hypium'
properties.image_credit: Roman theatre, Prusias ad Hypium, Konuralp, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Karadeniz Eregli
properties.one_line: Heraclea Pontica struck bronze coin under Trajan, including a dated issue from 114-116 CE that helps anchor the chronology of the whole regional currency of Bithynia and Pontus. Colonists from Megara had founded the city on this Black Sea harbor nearly seven centuries earlier, and it once ruled a wide stretch of the southern coast as an independent Hellenistic kingdom before Rome absorbed it. Under Trajan its mint output made up close to a sixth of all known coin emissions from the province's fourteen minting cities.
sources: RPC III 1161-1177, esp. 1176, Trajan, Heraclea Pontica
Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2024.07.03, 'Roman provincial coinage of Bithynia and Pontus during the reign of Trajan'
properties.image_credit: Historical map of Heraclea Pontica · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Kadikoy
properties.one_line: Chalcedon struck bronze coin under Trajan as one of Bithynia's oldest cities, founded by Greek settlers from Megara more than seven centuries before his reign. Ancient writers mocked its founders as 'the blind' for choosing this shore when the far richer harbor of Byzantium sat empty just across the strait. Excavations beneath the modern Haydarpasa train station have since turned up ancient bath complexes buried under the city for two thousand years.
sources: RPC III 1060-1061, Trajan, Chalcedon
The Archaeologist, 'Unearthing the Secrets of Ancient Chalcedon Beneath Modern Kadikoy'
properties.image_credit: 19th-century engraving of the Council of Chalcedon · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Alasehir
properties.one_line: Philadelphia, founded by King Attalus II and named for his devotion to his brother, struck civic bronze under Trajan showing the goddess Cybele enthroned with a lion at her feet. Frequent earthquakes had shaken the city so often in earlier centuries that Rome once excused it from paying tribute. The Book of Revelation's letter to the seven churches of Asia names Philadelphia as the one church Christ found no fault in.
sources: RPC III 2376/2377, Trajan, Philadelphia, Lydia
GRPC Lydia III 245-248
properties.image_credit: Ruins at Alasehir (ancient Philadelphia), Turkey · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Corinth
properties.one_line: Corinth struck civic bronze under Trajan a century and a half after Julius Caesar refounded the city as a Roman colony on ground the Greeks had abandoned since 146 BCE. Its coin types pictured the temples ringing the forum, among them the Archaic Temple of Apollo, whose seven surviving Doric columns had already stood for roughly six hundred years by Trajan's reign. The colony's harbors on two seas made it one of the wealthiest trading cities in the province of Achaia.
sources: RPC III 111-112, Trajan, Corinth
Forum Ancient Coins NumisWiki, 'Corinth Coins and Cults'
properties.image_credit: Temple of Apollo, Corinth, Greece · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Nicopolis
properties.one_line: Nicopolis, the 'City of Victory' Augustus founded on the site of his own camp before the Battle of Actium, saw its civic mint flourish anew under Trajan, whose issues hailed him as savior of the city. Sometime between 103 and 114 CE Trajan split Epirus off from Achaia as its own imperial province, with Nicopolis as capital. Actium's naval battle, fought in the straits visible from the city walls, had decided who would rule the whole Roman world a century and a half earlier.
sources: RPC Online, type 8948, Trajan, Nicopolis, Epirus
Academia.edu, 'Actia Nicopolis. Coinage, Currency and Civic Identity (27BC - AD268)'
properties.image_credit: Roman aqueduct of Nicopolis, Preveza, Greece · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Anazarbus
properties.one_line: Anazarbus, calling itself Caesarea in its own official coin legends, struck bronze under Trajan dated to civic year 132, equal to 113-114 CE, pairing his portrait with that of his wife Plotina. The city would later become metropolis of Cilicia Secunda, but even under Trajan it already ranked as Cilicia's second city after Tarsus. A ring of hills studded with a much later Armenian fortress still frames the wide plain where the ancient ruins spread today.
sources: RPC III 3369, 3370, Trajan and Plotina, Anazarbus (as Caesarea Anazarbus)
CNG Coin Shop, 'CILICIA, Anazarbus (as Caesarea Anazarbus). Trajan, with Plotina'
properties.image_credit: General view of the ruins of Anazarbus, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Tios
properties.one_line: Tium struck bronze under Trajan as a small but independent mint among the fourteen minting cities of Bithynia and Pontus, its dies skipping the shared regional designs some neighboring towns adopted. Milesian colonists had founded the city at the mouth of the Billaeus river in the 7th century BCE, centuries before Rome existed. Its harbor shipped timber cut from the forests of the Bithynian interior across the Black Sea.
sources: RPC III 1178-1190, Trajan, Tium
properties.image_credit: Tios (Tium) ancient city site, Filyos, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons
